title: Antony and Cleopatra
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Alexandria. A Room in Cleopatra's palace
about:
Mark Antony is one of three rulers of the Roman world, but he has spent the last year in Alexandria with Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, neglecting his duties. News arrives that his wife Fulvia has died and that the young Octavius Caesar and the third triumvir Lepidus need him in Rome. Antony tears himself away, returns to Rome, marries Caesar's sister Octavia for political reasons, and almost immediately goes back to Cleopatra. Caesar, slighted, marches on them.

The play follows Antony and Cleopatra through the naval defeat at Actium, where Cleopatra's ships flee and Antony follows her. It follows them through one more failed land battle, through Cleopatra's false report of her own death, through Antony falling on his sword in a botched suicide, through his death in Cleopatra's monument, through Caesar's offer to take her back to Rome as a captive, and through Cleopatra's decision to die by snakebite rather than be paraded through the streets.

Shakespeare wrote the play around 1606, drawing on Plutarch's Life of Antony. He gave it forty-two scenes — twice as many as most of his other tragedies — and let it move across the entire Mediterranean: Alexandria, Rome, Sicily, Athens, Messina, Actium. It is the most expansive of the tragedies, and the only one whose central couple are not young people but middle-aged rulers who have been famous for a long time and know what they are losing.

angleCards.title: Cleopatra.
angleCards.text: Cleopatra is Shakespeare's most fully realised woman — funny, jealous, theatrical, capable of being a queen and a girlfriend in the same scene. Watch her with attention. There is no other female part in the canon like her.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Cleopatra through the play as one of Shakespeare's most fully imagined characters: her temper, her theatre, her politics, and the ending she chooses for herself.

angleCards.title: Rome and Egypt.
angleCards.text: The play moves between two whole worlds: the cold Roman politics of Caesar and the heated Egyptian sensuality of Cleopatra's court. Each scene tilts the play toward one or the other. Watch which world wins, and when.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play as a contest between two whole ways of life — Roman duty and Egyptian pleasure — and see what Shakespeare gains and gives up in each.

angleCards.title: Antony's collapse.
angleCards.text: Antony is one of the three most powerful men in the world at the start of the play. He spends five acts losing every advantage he has, mostly because he cannot stay away from Cleopatra. The play asks whether that is a failure or a choice.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track Antony's decline scene by scene and decide whether the play shows him as ruined by love or as choosing what he most wants over what he is supposed to want.

angleCards.title: Caesar wins.
angleCards.text: Octavius Caesar — cold, young, calculating, the future Augustus — is the winner of the entire play. He is also the figure Shakespeare gives the least pleasure. The contrast between victor and losers is the play's quiet argument.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Octavius Caesar as the play's deliberate counterweight to Antony and Cleopatra: what kind of figure wins, and what the play thinks of his winning.

cast.name: Mark Antony
cast.description: One of the three rulers of the Roman world after the assassination of Julius Caesar, a great general past his best, a famous man losing his nerve. He has spent the last year in Egypt with Cleopatra and cannot keep away from her, even when his career and his life depend on it.

cast.name: Cleopatra
cast.description: The last queen of Egypt, in her late thirties when the play opens, witty, vain, theatrical, and harder to read than any other character in Shakespeare. She has already been the lover of Julius Caesar and is now the lover of Antony. The play gives her some of the best verse in the canon.

cast.name: Octavius Caesar
cast.description: Adoptive son of Julius Caesar and the future Emperor Augustus, in his early twenties at the start of the play. Cold, deliberate, and patient. He is the man for whom history is going to work out, and the play handles him accordingly: without affection.

cast.name: Enobarbus
cast.description: A Roman soldier who has followed Antony through every campaign, knows Cleopatra better than anyone, and gives the play its most famous description of her ('The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne…'). When he finally judges Antony has lost his judgement, he deserts to Caesar, then dies of his own remorse.

cast.name: Octavia
cast.description: A virtuous Roman lady whom Antony marries to cement the alliance with her brother. She is no rival to Cleopatra and never tries to be. Antony abandons her, which gives Caesar the public grievance he needs.

cast.name: Charmian
cast.description: Cleopatra's closest waiting woman, sharp, devoted, present in nearly every scene Cleopatra has. She is with her queen at the end and dies arranging Cleopatra's crown the moment after her mistress has stopped breathing.

acclaim.quote: This is the most wonderful of all Shakespeare's plays.
acclaim.context: Lectures on Shakespeare, on Antony and Cleopatra, 1813

acclaim.quote: Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety.
acclaim.context: Shakespeare's most quoted description of Cleopatra

whyItMatters.title: Cleopatra
whyItMatters.body: Shakespeare wrote almost no major roles for women. The four big tragedies — Hamlet, Lear, Othello, Macbeth — have one woman each who matters, and three of them are dead by Act 4. Antony and Cleopatra is the exception. Cleopatra is on stage as much as Antony, has at least as many lines as he does, dominates the play's last act on her own after he is gone, and is given the verse and the death scene of a Shakespeare tragic hero. She is also one of the only major Shakespeare characters who is comic and tragic at the same time: she plays jokes on her own servants, fakes her own death to manipulate her lover, jumps from a tantrum to a state speech in the same breath. T. S. Eliot called Othello's last speech the moment when he is 'cheering himself up.' Cleopatra is the only character in Shakespeare who can do that on her own behalf, in real time, while the audience laughs and is moved at once. The play is famous because of what Shakespeare gave to its lead, and because no one else in his work, before or after, gets the same gift.

whyItMatters.title: Two Worlds, Forty-Two Scenes
whyItMatters.body: Antony and Cleopatra has more scenes than any other Shakespeare tragedy by a wide margin. The play moves between Alexandria and Rome and a half-dozen other places on the Mediterranean rim — Misenum, Athens, Actium, Pompey's galley, the desert outside Alexandria — and changes location, often, every two minutes. This is deliberate. Shakespeare is staging a contest between two whole worlds: Rome, where men work, plan, calculate, and treat love as a distraction from politics; Egypt, where the politics is incidental and the love is the main event. The cuts between scenes do the comparison without comment. A long erotic exchange in Cleopatra's palace is followed by a cold council in Caesar's tent; a Roman victory is followed by an Egyptian feast. Audiences feel the play as restless, almost cinematic — and it has been a director's playground for that reason since the nineteenth century. Whatever you think of the affair at the centre, the play's structural argument is one of Shakespeare's most modern: the world is more than one place and one rhythm, and the choice between them is real.

whyItMatters.title: Two Suicides, No Apology
whyItMatters.body: Antony bungles his suicide. He gets bad information — a false report that Cleopatra has killed herself — and falls on his sword in the wrong way, half-killing himself; his servants refuse to finish the job; he is hauled, dying, up into Cleopatra's monument on ropes; he dies kissing her in front of her servants. It is the most undignified death of any Shakespeare hero. Cleopatra's death, in the play's final scene, is the opposite: orchestrated, theatrical, slow. She bathes and dresses and crowns herself and lets a Clown bring her a basket of figs with an asp inside; she dies upright on her throne in full royal costume, her women dying around her, while Caesar's men break into the chamber too late. Shakespeare set the two deaths against each other on purpose. Antony, the great Roman, dies a comedy of errors; Cleopatra, the woman the Romans dismissed as a distraction, dies the death they would all have wanted. The contrast is the play's last and most pointed line — and the reason this play, almost alone among the tragedies, gives its woman the last word.
